title: Ventilatory thresholds
goal: Find VT1 and VT2 from ventilatory equivalents and end-tidal pressures, explain what causes each, and judge how they relate to lactate thresholds and critical power.

steps.title: Ventilatory equivalents: air per litre of gas
steps.text:
A [ventilatory equivalent](g:ventilatory-equivalent) is the air you breathe per litre of gas exchanged:

- **V̇E/V̇O₂**: litres of air per litre of O₂ taken up.
- **V̇E/V̇CO₂**: litres of air per litre of CO₂ breathed out.

The litres cancel, so both are plain numbers. In a ramp test a [metabolic cart](g:metabolic-cart) plots them breath by breath, with the partial pressures at the end of each breath out ([end-tidal](g:end-tidal) PETO₂ and PETCO₂).

Read them like fuel use: a rising V̇E/V̇O₂ means you pay more air for each litre of O₂. Breathing tracks CO₂ (last lesson), so as intensity rises the two ratios part ways at two points: the ventilatory thresholds.

steps.title: Two ratios from one breath sample
steps.problem: In a ramp test a rider breathes 60 L·min⁻¹ while taking up 2.5 L·min⁻¹ of O₂ and breathing out 2.3 L·min⁻¹ of CO₂. Find both ventilatory equivalents.
steps: V̇E/V̇O₂ = 60 ÷ 2.5 = 24: 24 L of air for each litre of O₂.
V̇E/V̇CO₂ = 60 ÷ 2.3 = 26.1: 26.1 L of air for each litre of CO₂.
Air goes on top: the ratio is ventilation divided by gas exchanged, never the other way round.

steps.title: VT1: the first bend
steps.text:
The first ventilatory threshold ([VT1](g:vt1)) is where V̇E/V̇O₂ and PETO₂ start to rise while V̇E/V̇CO₂ does not [[c:vt1-criteria]].

Why? As work rises, more H⁺ is made. Blood bicarbonate buffers it and releases extra CO₂, which raises V̇CO₂ and ventilation [[c:buffer-co2]]. Breathing follows CO₂, so V̇E pulls ahead of V̇O₂ but stays in step with V̇CO₂.

The matching bend in V̇CO₂ against V̇O₂, the [gas exchange threshold](g:gas-exchange-threshold), is the non-invasive estimate of the lactate threshold. It doesn't mean the muscle is short of O₂ [[c:not-anoxia]].

Breathing frequency also speeds up at each threshold, so a breathing-rate sensor can hint at them [[c:fr-breaks]].

claims.text: VT1 is identified by a rise in V̇E/V̇O₂ and PETO₂ with no rise in V̇E/V̇CO₂.

evidence.quote: VT1 was determined using the criteria of an increase in both ventilatory equivalent of oxygen (V̇E/V̇O2) and end-tidal pressure of oxygen (PETO2) with no concomitant increase in ventilatory equivalent of carbon dioxide (V̇E/V̇CO2).

claims.text: H⁺ buffered by blood bicarbonate releases extra CO₂, raising V̇CO₂ and ventilation.

evidence.quote: increased H+ buffered by blood [HCO3−]→increased CO2 release from blood→increased V̇CO2 and pulmonary ventilation

claims.text: Insufficient O₂ is not the main cause of rising blood lactate; the gas exchange threshold remains a useful non-invasive estimate of the lactate threshold.

evidence.quote: It is now recognized that insufficient O2 is not the primary basis for lactataemia.
Non-invasive estimation of LT using the gas exchange threshold (non-linear increase of V̇CO2 versus V̇O2 ) remains important in exercise training and in the clinic

claims.text: Breathing frequency shows two distinct accelerations in a ramp test, matching the two gas-exchange thresholds.

evidence.quote: two separate and distinct accelerations in respiratory frequency (f (R)) during incremental work were observed

steps.title: VT2: respiratory compensation
steps.text:
Above VT1, V̇E/V̇CO₂ and PETCO₂ stay roughly flat for a while: breathing still matches CO₂. This stretch, from the first threshold to the second, is the [isocapnic buffering](g:isocapnic-buffering) period ('isocapnic' = same CO₂) [[c:isocapnic]].

At the second ventilatory threshold, VT2 or the [respiratory compensation point](g:respiratory-compensation-point) (RCP), V̇E/V̇CO₂ rises as well and PETCO₂ falls [[c:vt2-criteria]]. Breathing now outruns CO₂ output: the compensatory hyperventilation of the last lesson, driving PCO₂ down to limit the fall in pH.

To tell them apart, look at V̇E/V̇CO₂: flat at VT1, rising at VT2.

claims.text: The isocapnic buffering period runs from the first threshold (anaerobic threshold) to the respiratory compensation point.

evidence.quote: During cardiopulmonary exercise test, the isocapnic buffering period ranges between anaerobic threshold (AT) and respiratory compensation point (RCP).

claims.text: VT2 is identified by a rise in both V̇E/V̇O₂ and V̇E/V̇CO₂ with a fall in PETCO₂.

evidence.quote: VT2 was determined using the criteria of an increase in both the V̇E/V̇O2 and V̇E/V̇CO2 and a decrease in PETCO2

steps.title: Ventilatory and lactate thresholds
steps.text:
In 14 trained male cyclists, power at VT1 matched the first lactate threshold, and power at VT2 matched the lactate threshold + 2.0 mmol·L⁻¹. Both ventilatory thresholds were reliable from test to test (CV 1.6–3.5%) [[c:vt-lt-match]]. Lactate thresholds get their own module in tier 2.

RCP is often used as a stand-in for the highest sustainable intensity. In 12 men it came at the same V̇O₂ as [critical power](g:critical-power) and the [maximal lactate steady state](g:mlss) (MLSS), but at a higher power: 262 W against 226 and 223 W [[c:rcp-vo2-same]]. RCP power also rose with ramp speed, from 243 to 292 W, and agreed poorly with CP [[c:rcp-ramp]].

claims.text: In trained male cyclists, power at VT1 and VT2 matched power at the lactate threshold and at LT + 2.0 mmol·L⁻¹; ventilatory thresholds had CVs of 1.6–3.5%.

evidence.quote: Workloads at lactate threshold (LT) and LT+2.0 mMol·L-1 matched the ones for VT1 and VT2, respectively
Ventilatory thresholds show high reliability (CV = 1.6%-3.5%; r = 0.90-0.96; Bias = -1.8-2.9) except for RER = 1 and V-Slope

claims.text: RCP occurred at the same V̇O₂ as CP and MLSS, but at a higher power output in a ramp test.

evidence.quote: There were no differences (P > 0.05) among the V˙O2p values associated with CP, RCP, MLSS, and [HHb]BP
the PO associated with RCP (262 ± 48 W) and [HHb]BP (273 ± 41 W) were greater (P < 0.05) than both CP (226 ± 45 W) and MLSS (223 ± 39 W)

claims.text: The power at RCP rose with the ramp slope and agreed poorly with CP.

evidence.quote: Our data confirm that the external work rate associated with the RCP is labile and that these power outputs display poor measurement agreement with the CP.

debate.question: Can the respiratory compensation point stand in for critical power or MLSS?

sides.position: Yes, as a metabolic marker: RCP, CP and MLSS fall at the same V̇O₂, so they may reflect the same boundary.
No, as a power target: RCP power moves with the ramp protocol and agrees poorly with CP.

points: Ventilatory equivalents are air per litre of gas: V̇E/V̇O₂ and V̇E/V̇CO₂, plain numbers with no unit.
VT1: V̇E/V̇O₂ and PETO₂ rise while V̇E/V̇CO₂ stays flat, because bicarbonate buffering adds CO₂ and breathing follows CO₂.
Between VT1 and VT2 (isocapnic buffering) breathing still matches CO₂; at VT2, the respiratory compensation point, V̇E/V̇CO₂ rises and PETCO₂ falls.
VT1 tracks the first lactate threshold and VT2 a higher lactate point; neither marks a lack of O₂ in muscle.
RCP sits at the same V̇O₂ as CP and MLSS, but its ramp power depends on the protocol, so don't use it directly as a power target.

variants.stem: In a cyclist's ramp test, V̇E/V̇O₂ starts to rise at 210 W while V̇E/V̇CO₂ stays flat. Which threshold is that?

options.text: VT1, the first ventilatory threshold
options.why: Right: V̇E/V̇O₂ rising with V̇E/V̇CO₂ flat is the VT1 pattern.

options.text: VT2, the respiratory compensation point
options.why: At VT2 V̇E/V̇CO₂ rises too and PETCO₂ falls; here V̇E/V̇CO₂ is flat.

options.text: VO₂max
options.why: VO₂max is the top of the test, where V̇O₂ stops rising; the ratios don't define it.

options.text: No threshold: just noise in the data
options.why: A sustained rise in one ratio while the other stays flat is the classic VT1 signal, not noise.

variants.stem: In a runner's treadmill test, at 16 km/h V̇E/V̇CO₂ starts to rise and PETCO₂ falls. Which threshold is that?

options.text: VT2, the respiratory compensation point
options.why: Right: V̇E/V̇CO₂ rising and PETCO₂ falling means breathing now outruns CO₂ output.

options.text: VT1, the first ventilatory threshold
options.why: At VT1 V̇E/V̇CO₂ stays flat; only V̇E/V̇O₂ rises.

options.text: The start of isocapnic buffering
options.why: Isocapnic buffering is the stretch before this point, where V̇E/V̇CO₂ and PETCO₂ stay flat.

options.text: VO₂max
options.why: VO₂max is where V̇O₂ stops rising; it is defined by O₂ uptake, not by these ratios.

variants.stem: At 14 km/h a runner breathes 90 L·min⁻¹ and takes up 3.0 L·min⁻¹ of O₂. What is his V̇E/V̇O₂?

options.why: Right: 90 ÷ 3.0 = 30 L of air per litre of O₂.
This divides O₂ by air (3.0 ÷ 90). Air goes on top.
This multiplies (90 × 3.0); a ratio divides.
This subtracts (90 − 3.0); a ratio divides.

variants.solution: V̇E/V̇O₂ = 90 L·min⁻¹ ÷ 3.0 L·min⁻¹ = 30 (no unit: the litres cancel).

variants.stem: Near the top of a ramp test a cyclist breathes 120 L·min⁻¹ and breathes out 4.0 L·min⁻¹ of CO₂. What is her V̇E/V̇CO₂?

options.why: Right: 120 ÷ 4.0 = 30 L of air per litre of CO₂.
This divides CO₂ by air (4.0 ÷ 120). Air goes on top.
This multiplies (120 × 4.0); a ratio divides.
This subtracts (120 − 4.0); a ratio divides.

variants.stem: On the bike leg a triathlete breathes 70 L·min⁻¹ and takes up 2.8 L·min⁻¹ of O₂. What is his V̇E/V̇O₂?

options.why: Right: 70 ÷ 2.8 = 25 L of air per litre of O₂.
This divides O₂ by air (2.8 ÷ 70). Air goes on top.
This multiplies (70 × 2.8); a ratio divides.
This subtracts (70 − 2.8); a ratio divides.

variants.stem: Over two stages, a runner's V̇E/V̇O₂ rises from 25 to 30. What does that mean?

options.text: He now breathes more air for each litre of O₂ taken up
options.why: Right: the ratio is litres of air per litre of O₂, and it went up.

options.text: He now takes up more O₂ from each litre of air
options.why: The opposite: a higher ratio means less O₂ per litre of air.

options.text: His O₂ uptake has fallen
options.why: Not necessarily: V̇O₂ can keep rising while V̇E rises faster.

options.text: His lungs have become worse at diffusion
options.why: The ratio says nothing directly about diffusion; it compares air breathed with O₂ used.

variants.stem: At VT1, why does V̇E/V̇O₂ rise while V̇E/V̇CO₂ stays flat?

options.text: Buffering acid with bicarbonate adds CO₂, and breathing follows CO₂
options.why: Right: extra CO₂ raises V̇CO₂ and V̇E together, so V̇E pulls ahead of V̇O₂ only.

options.text: The muscles run out of O₂, so O₂ uptake falls
options.why: O₂ uptake keeps rising past VT1, and lack of O₂ is not the main cause of rising lactate.

options.text: The lungs start leaking O₂ back out
options.why: That doesn't happen: O₂ diffuses into the blood down its gradient.

options.text: Dead space suddenly grows
options.why: Dead space doesn't jump at VT1; the change comes from extra CO₂.

variants.stem: A coach tells a triathlete: "VT1 is where your muscles run out of oxygen." What is the best reply?

options.text: Not really: lack of O₂ isn't what raises lactate or CO₂ at VT1
options.why: Right: the extra CO₂ comes from buffering acid, and lactate rises with glycolytic flux, not muscle anoxia.

options.text: Yes: that is exactly why it's also called the anaerobic threshold
options.why: The name is old; the idea behind it (muscle anoxia) has not held up.

options.text: No: VT1 has nothing at all to do with blood lactate
options.why: VT1 tracks the lactate threshold closely; it just isn't caused by lack of O₂.

options.text: Yes, but only in runners, and not in cyclists or swimmers
options.why: The physiology is the same in every sport, and the anoxia idea fails in all of them.

variants.stem: A triathlete does a ramp test on the bike wearing a breathing-rate sensor. Her breathing frequency shows two clear accelerations. What could they mark?

options.text: Roughly her two ventilatory thresholds
options.why: Right: in cyclists, two accelerations in f matched the two gas-exchange thresholds.

options.text: Her VO₂max and her maximal heart rate
options.why: Both come at the end of the test; the accelerations come earlier, at the thresholds.

options.text: Only sensor noise: breathing rate is too variable
options.why: f is noisy breath to breath, but the two accelerations were consistent findings.

options.text: The end of warm-up and the start of fatigue
options.why: These are not defined physiological points; the accelerations line up with the thresholds.

variants.stem: Ramp test, stage by stage (V̇E/V̇O₂ ; V̇E/V̇CO₂ ; PETCO₂ in mmHg): 150 W: 22 ; 25 ; 42. 180 W: 22 ; 25 ; 43. 210 W: 25 ; 25 ; 43. 240 W: 27 ; 25 ; 43. 270 W: 31 ; 29 ; 39. Where are VT1 and VT2?

options.text: VT1 at 210 W, VT2 at 270 W
options.why: Right: at 210 W V̇E/V̇O₂ rises while V̇E/V̇CO₂ stays at 25; at 270 W V̇E/V̇CO₂ rises and PETCO₂ falls.

options.text: VT1 at 270 W, VT2 at 210 W
options.why: Reversed: VT1 is the first bend (V̇E/V̇O₂ alone), VT2 the second (V̇E/V̇CO₂ too).

options.text: VT1 at 180 W, VT2 at 210 W
options.why: 180 W is the last stage before any change; 210 W is VT1, where only V̇E/V̇O₂ rises.

options.text: VT1 at 240 W, VT2 at 270 W
options.why: V̇E/V̇O₂ already rose at 210 W; VT1 is where the rise starts.

variants.stem: Treadmill test, stage by stage (V̇E/V̇O₂ ; V̇E/V̇CO₂ ; PETCO₂ in mmHg): 12 km/h: 24 ; 26 ; 41. 13 km/h: 24 ; 26 ; 42. 14 km/h: 27 ; 26 ; 42. 15 km/h: 29 ; 26 ; 42. 16 km/h: 33 ; 30 ; 38. Where are VT1 and VT2?

options.text: VT1 at 14 km/h, VT2 at 16 km/h
options.why: Right: at 14 km/h V̇E/V̇O₂ rises while V̇E/V̇CO₂ stays at 26; at 16 km/h V̇E/V̇CO₂ rises and PETCO₂ falls.

options.text: VT1 at 16 km/h, VT2 at 14 km/h
options.why: Reversed: VT1 is the first bend (V̇E/V̇O₂ alone), VT2 the second (V̇E/V̇CO₂ too).

options.text: VT1 at 13 km/h, VT2 at 14 km/h
options.why: 13 km/h is the last stage before any change; 14 km/h is VT1.

options.text: VT1 at 15 km/h, VT2 at 16 km/h
options.why: V̇E/V̇O₂ already rose at 14 km/h; VT1 is where the rise starts.

variants.stem: In trained cyclists, how do the ventilatory thresholds line up with blood lactate?

options.text: VT1 with the first lactate threshold, VT2 with a higher lactate point
options.why: Right: VT1 matched the lactate threshold and VT2 matched the lactate threshold + 2.0 mmol·L⁻¹.

options.text: VT1 with the highest lactate, VT2 with resting lactate
options.why: Backwards and too extreme: VT1 is the lower threshold, near the first lactate rise.

options.text: Both with resting lactate
options.why: Lactate is above rest at both thresholds, more so at VT2.

options.text: Neither: ventilation and lactate are unrelated
options.why: They are related: both reflect the same rise in metabolic rate and acid load.

variants.stem: A rider's respiratory compensation point on a fast ramp (45 W·min⁻¹) is 300 W. His critical power is 250 W. Should he use 300 W as his target for a 40 km time trial?

options.text: No: RCP power rises with ramp speed and overshoots CP on fast ramps
options.why: Right: RCP power is protocol-dependent; on fast ramps it sat about 45 W above CP.

options.text: Yes: RCP is the most accurate marker of sustainable power
options.why: RCP power agreed poorly with CP and changed with the ramp; it isn't a reliable power target.

options.text: Yes, but only if he rides at RCP heart rate instead
options.why: Heart rate drifts in long efforts; that doesn't fix a power target that is too high.

options.text: No: RCP is always well below CP
options.why: On fast ramps RCP power is above CP, not below it.

variants.stem: In one study, RCP, critical power and MLSS all came at the same V̇O₂, but RCP came at a higher power (262 W against 226 and 223 W). Which conclusion do these data best support?

options.text: Same boundary, perhaps, but ramp RCP power isn't a steady power target
options.why: Right: same V̇O₂ points to the same boundary; the higher ramp power shows it isn't a direct power target.

options.text: RCP is a separate, higher boundary than critical power
options.why: The V̇O₂ values were the same, which argues for one boundary, not two.

options.text: CP and MLSS are wrong, and RCP is the true limit
options.why: Nothing shows CP or MLSS are wrong; they agreed with each other.

options.text: V̇O₂ values can't be compared from one test to another
options.why: The study compared V̇O₂ across tests on purpose; that is how the match was found.

variants.stem: A female runner reads that VT1 and VT2 match lactate thresholds closely, from a study of 14 trained male cyclists. What most limits applying it to her?

options.text: Only trained men, cycling, were tested, and n = 14 is small
options.why: Right: sex, sport and test mode differ from hers, and a small sample gives imprecise agreement.

options.text: Lactate can't be measured in runners
options.why: It can: finger or ear-lobe samples work on a treadmill.

options.text: The thresholds were unreliable from test to test
options.why: They were reliable (CV 1.6–3.5%); reliability isn't the problem.

options.text: Ventilatory thresholds only exist in cycling
options.why: They appear in any incremental test, running included.
